Dual Photoredox/Copper-Catalyzed Three-Component
Alkylcyanation of Alkenes and 1,4-Alkylcyanation of 1,3-Enynes
Employing Sulfoxonium Ylides as the Carbon Radical Precursors

ABSTRACT: A novel dual photoredox/copper-catalyzed three-component alkylcyanation of alkenes and 1,4-alkylcyanation of 1,3-
enynes have been developed. In this radical cyanoalkylation reaction, the photoredox induced alkyl radical from sulfoxonium ylides
adds to the carbon−carbon double bonds of styrenes or 1,3-enynes, and the generated benzylic or allenyl radicals couple with a
Cu(II) cyanide complex to achieve selective cyanation. The reaction exhibits high chemo- and regioselectivity and a wide substrate
scope, providing an efficient method for the synthesis of alkyl nitriles and allenyl nitriles in a single step.
A
lkenes have proven to be ideal building blocks in organic
chemistry due to their easy accessibility, abundance and
versatile reactivity.
1
Among various transformations of alkenes,
the difunctionalization of alkenes has been widely developed,
which allows the introduction of two functional groups to the
double bond of alkenes in a single step.
2
In particular, the
intermolecular three-component radical difunctionalization of
alkenes has become a powerful strategy for efficiently enhancing
molecular complexity.
3
Recently, the visible-light-induced
radical strategy has further matured the radical difunctionaliza-
tion of alkenes under environmentally benign mild conditions.
4
In this field, the dual photoredox/copper-catalyzed cyanoalky-
lation of alkenes has been reported.
5,6
However, it still faces
challenges due to the limited availability of alkyl radical
precursors and only N-hydroxyl phthalimide esters
5
and alkyl
bromides
6
can be used as carbon radical sources. In addition,
sulfur ylides are regarded as a kind of versatile building block in
organic synthesis due to their rich reactivity, high stability and
easy preparation.
7
With the development of photochemistry,
visible-light-induced photoredox carbon radical formation from
sulfur ylides via homolytic cleavage of C−S bonds has received
considerable attention in recent years.
8
However, to the best of
our knowledge, the visible-light-induced cyanoalkylation of
alkenes with carbon radicals generated from sulfoxonium ylides
has not been reported. Thus, realizing the dual photoredox/
metal-catalyzed cyanoalkylation of alkenes with novel alkyl
radical precursors, especially for the radical cyanoalkylation of
alkenes with sulfoxonium ylides and TMSCN, is highly desired.
Allenes represent important structural units found frequently
in many natural products, pharmaceuticals, and molecular
materials.
9
Moreover, they are also useful and versatile building
blocks for the synthesis of diverse and valuable compounds in
organic synthesis.
10
Consequently, many methods for the
synthesis of allenes have been developed.
11
Among these, the
1,4-difunctionalization of 1,3-enynes is considered to be one of
the best methods to construct multisubstituted allenes because
two functionalities are installed in a single step.
12−19
In recent
years, there has been remarkable progress in photoredox- and
transition metal-catalyzed radical 1,4-difunctionalization of 1,3-
enynes for the synthesis of allenes.
13−19
In this context, the
radical-mediated 1,4-alkylcyanation of 1,3-enynes employing
diacyl peroxides,
14
fluoroalkyl halides,
15

(NHP) esters,

alkylcyanation of 1,3-enynes with novel carbon radical

corresponding carbonyl-containing alkyl nitriles 3aa−l in good
to high yields. Similarly, pentafluorostyrene 2m was also
compatible with this cyanoalkylation reaction and gave the
desired product 3am in 52% yield. Furthermore, the
difunctionalization proceeded well with 4-vinylpyridine 2n and
2-vinylnaphthalene 2o, with the generation of alkyl nitriles 3an
and 3ao in 63% and 60% yields, respectively. However, no
desired products were observed when pent-4-en-1-ylbenzene, 2-
bromobut-1-ene or ethene-1,1-diyldibenzene was used as a
coupling partner. A scale-up reaction of 1a (21.0 mmol), 2a (7.0
mmol) and TMSCN (21.0 mmol) was carried out for 48 h under
otherwise identical conditions, affording 1.76 g of the product
3aa in 74% yield.
Next, the substrate scope of sulfoxonium ylides 1 was
evaluated. As shown in Table 3, various benzoyl-substituted
sulfoxonium ylides 1b−j bearing electron-donating, electron-
withdrawing and electron-neutral substituents on the aromatic
ring, could react with 2a and TMSCN to give the corresponding
alkyl nitriles 3b−ja in 30−72% yields. In this transformation, a
variety of functional groups, such as alkyl, trifluoromethoxy,
fluorine, chlorine, and bromine, were tolerated. Moreover, this
reaction proceeded well with heteroaryl-substituted sulfoxo-
nium ylide 1k and 2-naphthyl-substituted sulfoxonium ylide 1l
to deliver desired products 3ka and 3la in 47% and 60% yields,
respectively. Notably, even employing sulfur ylide 1h′ as a
carbon radical source, the desired product 3ha was obtained in
45% yield. However, no desired product was obtained when
cyclohexylacyl-substituted sulfoxonium ylide was employed as
the radical precursor.

To further probe the reaction mechanisms, some control
experiments were investigated (Scheme 1). We found that the
formation of 3aa was drastically reduced from 76% to 11% in the
presence of 2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidinooxy (TEMPO, 3.0
equiv) under the optimized condition, whereas the TEMPO-
trapped-carbonyl carbon radical compound 6 was obtained in
81% yield ((a)). When the reaction of 1a, TMSCN and (1-
cyclopropylvinyl)benzene 7 as a radical clock was performed
under the standard conditions, the product 8 was obtained in
35% yield ((b)). The product 9 generated by the self-coupling of
carbonyl carbon radical A (Scheme 3) was formed in 17% yield
when 1b was treated under the standard condition ((c)). As
anticipated, visible light irradiation is critical for this
alkylcyanation of alkene 2a and 1,4-alkylcyanation of 1,3-
enyne 4j ((d and f)). Similarly, only a trace amount of 5j was
observed for the 1,4-alkylcyanation reaction of 1a, 4j and
TMSCN in the presence of TEMPO (3.0 equiv) and product 6
was also produced in 78% yield ((e)). These experimental
results demonstrate that the alkylcyanation reaction might be a
radical process and that carbonyl carbon radical A might be
generated during the reaction. The product 3aa was obtained in

product 3aa was generated in 67% and 12% yields ((h) and (i)),

In conclusion, we have developed a novel dual photoredox-
and copper-catalyzed three-component alkylcyanation of
alkenes with TMSCN and sulfoxonium ylides for the first
time. In addition, 1,3-enynes could also be compatible with the
reaction system to carry out the three-component 1,4-
alkylcyanation reaction. The reaction exhibits high chemo-
and regioselectivity and wide substrate scope and provides an
efficient route to the synthesis of carbonyl-containing alkyl
nitriles and allenyl nitriles in a single step. Mechanistic studies
also prove that sulfoxonium ylides serve as carbon-centered
radical precursors and will inspire new opportunities for the
design of radical-mediated multicomponent reactions. Further
application of sulfur ylides is under investigation in our lab.
